children: By Ian Hodgson, Konrad Putzier and Rebecca Cadenhead
Americans are straining under sky-high grocery prices. The pain might get worse.

Food costs rose at the fastest rate in six months in October, driven by snarled supply chains, unpredictable weather and, increasingly, high fuel prices because of the Iran war. The cost of restaurant meals rose at the fastest pace since December 2025.
And now, more farmers and big food manufacturers are preparing to pass higher energy costs on to consumers.
"The worst is yet to come," said Scotiabank economist Olivier Gervais.

At the Hunts Point Produce Market in the Bronx, N.Y., which distributes fresh fruits and vegetables to thousands of grocery stores across the Northeast, wholesalers have run out of room to shoulder rising diesel costs. "We absorb what we can, but a lot of it gets passed to the consumer because there's not a lot of margin," said Stefanie Katzman, the fourth-generation chief executive of S. Katzman Produce.

At food giant Kraft Heinz, CEO Steve Cahillane warned last week that price increases across its portfolio were coming in 2027. "The cost pressure is everywhere," he said, adding that while "the consumer is in a fragile state, there's clearly more inflation."

U.S. grocery prices in October rose 0.4% from the previous month, the Labor Department said Tuesday, ending several months of relatively benign food inflation. Prices of fresh food like fruit and vegetables increased at an even greater rate.
The sharpest hits landed on everyday dinner staples: Lettuce jumped 8% in October alone, while beef steaks climbed 1.7%, butter jumped 2% and cheese rose 1.3%.

The latest pickup in food prices comes as Americans are already struggling with stretches of elevated inflation as grocery prices soared by more than 20% in the years following the Covid-19 pandemic and have continued to climb since.

Food costs matter more to voters than other categories because groceries are a necessity. Those prices are also highly visible: Most Americans go shopping weekly. "Everybody feels them, even if they're small increases," said Bernhard Dalheimer, an agricultural economist at Purdue University. High food costs contributed to the sense of voter frustration that swept Democrats to victory in the midterm elections. In an ABC News poll of House voters, 59% of respondents said they were unhappy about grocery prices.

Food prices are volatile, and economists caution that one month's increase doesn't necessarily mean the costs will keep rising. Still, pressures are mounting as high diesel prices, freight surcharges and rising agricultural costs grind through production networks.

Crude oil prices have dropped from recent peaks, but the fuel that powers food distribution has stayed stubbornly expensive. Retail diesel prices have increased by more than 66% since the start of the war in Iran, reaching a record high of $6.53 in September.

The cost of transportation services has increased by 20% since the start of the year, according to the Labor Department, signaling that trucking and logistics carriers are passing elevated diesel bills down the line to wholesalers and processors. That pressure is already registering for distributors as wholesale food prices jumped 1.3% in October, the sharpest monthly increase in the producer-price index since February.

Fresh fruit is already costlier to import, a spokesperson for fresh fruit and vegetable distributor Dole said, as expensive fuel inflates shipping, fertilizer and packaging costs. Weather conditions caused by a powerful El Niño have only compounded the strain.
"Bananas cannot stay and cannot be sustainable at these prices, at this level," said fruit-and-vegetable distributor Del Monte's CEO Mohammad Abu-Ghazaleh on a recent earnings call.

Food-supply chains move slowly and sellers will eat higher costs for as long as possible before raising consumer prices, Gervais of Scotiabank said. While freight costs react immediately, the peak price impact on grocery shelves takes 12 to 18 months to fully filter through production and distribution markets.
"It's too early to say if pass-through has started," Gervais said.

The delay reflects the mechanics of producing and moving food, said Georgetown University economist Sharat Ganapati. Grocery chains often negotiate prices months in advance and retailers will absorb costs as long as possible before repricing.
"That will attenuate the immediate effect," he said, "but the pressure builds up."

Early cracks are already appearing in categories with short supply chains, where perishable goods can't wait out freight swings in cold storage. In October, consumer prices for fresh vegetables jumped 2.2%.

Farm-level costs threaten to compound the squeeze over the next year. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz also pushed up fertilizer prices because Qatar is a key producer. Prices are still elevated just as farmers are starting to buy for spring planting.
"This is something that could drive food prices over the next year," Dalheimer, the economist, said.

Campbell's chief financial officer, Todd Cunfer, told investors in September that the company raised prices across 60% of its product portfolio in a bid to manage rising costs. Previously, Campbell's had shut down two snack plants and cut more than 550 salaried jobs — roughly 13% of its corporate workforce.
But with manufacturers exhausting internal cuts and long-term contracts rolling over, the ability of retailers to shield customers from higher prices is wearing thin.

Lilia Vailikit, a 71-year-old retired nurse in South Florida, is already feeling the pain. She said she strains to make ends meet with her monthly Social Security payments, and it doesn't help that gas prices and her condo maintenance are also up. As a result of belt-tightening, she can no longer make trips to her native Philippines every year or two.
"Every time I go to the store, it's more expensive," she said. "Groceries — Jesus Christ."
